item.title: Three People Are Killed at a Minnesota Day Care Center
item.description:
Two adults and a child were killed Wednesday morning at a small day care center in a Minneapolis suburb, police officials said.

The three victims were members of a family, Brent Johnson, the police chief in Hopkins, Minn., told reporters. The assailant, a man, was among those who died, Chief Johnson said.

Chief Johnson called the attack a domestic situation and said investigators did not believe there was a continuing threat. The killings happened around 9 a.m., he said. Chief Johnson said that investigators believe that the two adults who died owned the day care, which operated inside their home.

Six other children who were at the in-home day care center were reunited with their parents, he said.

“This is a horrific, tragic situation for any community, especially here in Hopkins, where we don’t see this type of crime,” Chief Johnson said.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

item.title: With Big Choices Ahead, Ocasio-Cortez Navigates New Territory
item.description:
Since she won her first election in 2018 at 28, becoming the youngest woman ever elected to Congress, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Democrat of New York, has been a political obsession for fans to adore and critics to abhor.

Her body, her weight, the clothes she wore in magazine shoots, her lipstick, her endorsements, her ill-fated decision to attend the Met Gala in a “tax the rich” gown, have been parsed and picked apart, in ways she has described as sometimes “dehumanizing” even when that parsing was coming from her supporters.

One area where she was insulated from such scrutiny was her love life: Ms. Ocasio-Cortez arrived on the national political scene with her boyfriend from college, Riley Roberts, by her side. And he stayed there as she became one of the most consequential women in American politics, a burly redhead who stood mostly outside the frame of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s public life. In 2022, her team announced in a fund-raising email that the couple was engaged.

Four years later, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is at a new juncture. Her relationship with Mr. Roberts quietly ended some time ago and her decision to livestream her egg-freezing journey has forced to the forefront an uncomfortable topic for a lawmaker who is both unusually open and incredibly private: a breakup that she had never broadcast, despite giving her followers a sense that they are often along with her for the ride.

The new information about Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s private life is coming alongside a spate of speculation that she’s preparing to run for president. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, who has said she hasn’t ruled out a presidential run or a run for Senate, could now be navigating a possible national or statewide campaign as a young, world-famous, single woman, a profile that would only intensify the ideological and cultural debates that swirl around her.

The reality of that new level of exposure became apparent on Tuesday night after a reporter for Puck and TMZ reported that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had split with Mr. Roberts, which was confirmed to The New York Times by multiple people knowledgeable about her personal life. Her relationship status was not new, but public disclosure of it all but broke the internet.

“All the single left-wing men in this city are about to line up nightly for dinner in her district until she picks one like the suitors in The Odyssey,” Asad Dandia, a Brooklyn-based community organizer, wrote on X.

As early as 2020, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was open about struggling to find a balance between life and work. “I’m sitting here, I’m like, Do I freeze my eggs? Can I afford to do that?” she asked in an interview with Vanity Fair that year. “My orthodontist was telling me about how she was doing I.V.F., and I’m, like, asking her what her experience is like.”

Diana Z. O’Brien, chair of women, gender and sexuality studies at Washington University in St. Louis, said that as a 36-year-old progressive lightning rod with political ambitions outside of the House, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had no real choice but to make public her decision to freeze her eggs — and then, by association, her breakup.

“If she says nothing, then people will infer that she’s making a decision to de-prioritize family,” Ms. O’Brien said.

Ms. O’Brien said it was inevitable that with that disclosure came the less comfortable one, about her relationship status.

“It came up for Senator Cory Booker before he was married, so it will definitely come up for a woman,” she said. “This allows her to say, ‘yes, I’m single right now, but that doesn’t mean I intend to be child-free or single forever.’ It counterbalances a narrative that would try to portray her as a very particular type of leftist single woman who hates men.”

David Axelrod, the former top adviser to President Barack Obama, said that being an unmarried woman “probably adds a degree of difficulty” to any run she might make to become the first woman elected president, although he noted that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez operates in her own orbit and according to her own rules because of her “unique ability to take people along for the ride in a way that is personally connecting.”

He added: “The bigger question to me is whether this is a ride she wants or needs to take at this stage because it would require an absolute surrender of so much of her life.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has not publicly addressed the end of her relationship, but that has not stopped anyone from weighing in on it. Conservatives piled on to criticize her for putting her political ambitions above her relationship. And group chats lit up with ideas for who Ms. Ocasio-Cortez might date without their politics being picked apart: A chef? A musician? A Knick?

On Capitol Hill, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s colleagues have long known she was no longer engaged. And she has not exactly hidden it. For one thing, she doesn’t wear an engagement ring. But she has also not gone public about her relationship status or whether she is dating again.

When a reporter asked her on Sunday what her fiancé thought of her decision to freeze her eggs, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez sidestepped the question, noting only that “all of my loved ones have been very supportive.” Her chief of staff, Mike Casca, did not respond to a request for comment for this piece.

But the reality is that being a prominent young, single woman lawmaker draws attention and poses challenges that men with a similar profile might not encounter, including reproductive choices.

Representative Yassamin Ansari, the 34-year-old Democrat from Arizona, said dating can be difficult when she feels like she is never in one place for long.

“I have my Arizona life and I have my D.C. life and I never feel like I’m rooted somewhere,” she said in an interview. Ms. Ansari said she was in a relationship when she was first elected in 2024, but that it ended in part because “it was super difficult for me to prioritize that on top of everything else going on.” As for dating, she said she prefers meeting people in real life and that “the apps do make me nervous. The job responsibilities make everything more challenging.”

She added: “I will probably freeze my eggs, too.”

For Ms. Ocasio-Cortez the scrutiny exists at another level. Over the years, she has given her followers a sense of shared intimacy by allowing them to watch her make black bean soup and assemble IKEA furniture on social media while talking about policy and answering questions about her daily routines. She participated in an emotional livestream after the Jan. 6 mob attack on the Capitol, describing in detail the trauma she felt from the day.

But being vulnerable and prominent has not been without cost, or easy.

“I miss being able to go outside in sweats,” she told Time magazine in 2019, just after she was elected. “I can’t go anywhere in public and just be a person without a lot of people watching everything I do.”

After she was criticized for attending the Met Gala, despite her Democratic Socialist politics, she wrote online: “I and my body have been so heavily and relentlessly policed from all corners politically since the moment I won my election.”

Jessica Valenti, the feminist writer who publishes the popular newsletter, “Abortion, Every Day,” said that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was so triggering to the right because she represents a direct affront to their well-funded message that women should get married young and have children young.

“Here, you have this very beautiful, very powerful woman, who is creating the life that she wants and appears to be very happy,” she said. “A very big part of the conservative Republican agenda right now is targeting young women. The last thing they need is a young woman modeling what a life could look like that they are so desperate to stop.”

Ms. Valenti said that “to a certain group of people, there is nothing A.O.C. could ever do, nothing would be OK with them” and that will likely carry into her personal life. “Regardless of who she dates,” she said, “how public she is or how private she is, someone is going to have an issue with it.”

Indeed, Allie Beth Stuckey, a conservative commentator, wrote online that Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was “glamorizing the lie that women can have it all. You can’t. Biology is real and how you order your life makes or breaks your future.” Ms. Stuckey’s criticism was emblematic of the view from the Christian right on reproductive rights like egg-freezing and I.V.F., which remains culturally contested ground when it comes to judging the personal choices of a young lawmaker.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has long been self-aware about the strangeness of growing up in a political petri dish. In her livestream on Sunday, she told her followers that the downside of being elected as a young person is “you have to then grow up in the public eye in a time that most people get to grow more privately.”

She added: “when you get elected later in life, you’ve made all of your mistakes in private. When you get elected when you’re young, you have to do all of that in public.”

As she prepared to inject her exposed belly with a fertility shot, she warned viewers, “don’t be weird about this,” no doubt knowing full well that they almost certainly would be.

item.title: 3 Ex-Georgia Deputies Used Flock Cameras to Stalk People, Sheriff Says
item.description:
Three former Georgia sheriff’s deputies have been arrested on charges that they used Flock cameras to stalk people, the latest cases to raise concerns about potential abuse involving the widely used network of license-plate readers.

The Bibb County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement that an internal audit conducted with help from Flock revealed that the deputies had used the camera system’s license plate data for “personal, non-law-enforcement purposes.”

All three were involved in separate incidents tracking people with whom they had a “personal relationship at the time,” the sheriff’s office said.

The deputies were arrested on Monday on charges that included stalking, prohibited use of license plate data and violating their oaths as public officers. They have since been released on bond.

Two of those charged, Toni Lewis and Coznavian Stubbs, resigned from their positions as patrol deputies during the investigation, and the third, Joseph Callaway, resigned as a K-9 deputy shortly after his arrest, the office said.

The Bibb County sheriff, David Davis, said that a tool that Flock introduced in April, called Audit Assistance, had uncovered the deputies’ misuse of the system. Flock says the tool continuously monitors system activity and flags search patterns that “fall outside an agency’s typical usage,” allowing police departments to identify instances of potential abuse.

“I was saddened by it,” Sheriff Davis said in an interview on Wednesday. “Each one of these deputies were good deputies who had been here for several years and were doing a good job. However, they made some poor decisions and crossed the line.”

Mr. Stubbs said on Wednesday that he had been accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his girlfriend but that he had only used the system to look up the license plate on his own car. The case, he said, had been “blown way out” of proportion.

Mr. Callaway declined to comment on the charges. Ms. Lewis could not be reached at phone numbers listed under her name, and it was not immediately clear if she had a lawyer.

A national debate has been brewing over Flock cameras, which can be found on roads in every state but Alaska. About 7,000 law enforcement agencies, or 40 percent of all departments in the United States, have contracts with the company, which is based in Atlanta.

Flock’s cameras, which use artificial intelligence to automatically identify and track vehicles, are connected, creating a vast, searchable network. Investigators have praised the system as a valuable tool that helps them track down stolen cars, find missing or wanted people and solve crimes

Critics, including local watchdog groups and civil liberties organizations, have said the cameras create an umbrella of surveillance that can be easily misused.

In Milwaukee, an officer was charged with using camera data to track someone he was dating and the person’s ex. In Texas, an officer used the cameras to track a woman across state lines who was suspected of self-administering an abortion. In Georgia, a former Polk County officer was charged last week with using the camera system “for non-law-enforcement purposes.” Other officers across the country have been disciplined or fired for tracking romantic partners.

In Bibb County, Ga., which is home to about 158,000 people and includes Macon, Sheriff Davis announced in June 2023 that his office had been awarded a $1.6 million state grant to deploy Flock cameras and to set up a Strategic Information Center to monitor the license-plate data they collect.

Sheriff Davis said that at one more than 220 deputies had access to the cameras, but that number had since been cut to around 160. He said he planned to work with community members to ensure the system is only used for legitimate investigations.

“We will continue to monitor and audit the use of this technology and take appropriate action whenever those standards are violated,” Sheriff Davis said in a statement. “Protecting the public also means protecting the public’s trust.”

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Two Killed in Military Helicopter Crash Near Fort Hood in Texas
item.description:
Two people died in a military helicopter crash on Wednesday outside Fort Hood in Texas, the authorities said.

The Bell County Sheriff’s Office received a 911 call just after 1:30 p.m. about a helicopter crash in Salado, a small town about 20 miles southeast of Fort Hood, a United States Army base.

The two people were pronounced dead around 2:30 p.m. local time, said Cliff Coleman, a spokesman for the sheriff’s office. He directed questions about the identity of the two people to the military.

“You could tell it was a violent crash,” Mr. Coleman said.

Officials at Fort Hood did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In a news release, U.S. Army officials said the aircraft involved in the crash, an AH-64 Apache attack helicopter, was based at Fort Hood.

The crash caused a blaze in the dry fields where it landed and law enforcement officials evacuated several area residents, Mr. Coleman said.

The fire was not immediately contained, he said.

A number of military helicopters have crashed in Texas in recent decades. In 2015, four soldiers died when a Black Hawk helicopter crashed about 60 miles north of Austin. In 2004, a brigadier general and six soldiers in Texarkana, Texas, also aboard a Black Hawk, crashed into a transmission tower and died.

item.title: Johanna Fernández, Historian of the Young Lords, Dies at 55
item.description:
Johanna Fernández, a Dominican American historian whose authoritative book about the Young Lords helped revive the legacy of that leftist collective, a revolutionary Latino counterpart to the Black Panthers, died on July 30 in Manhattan. She was 55.

Her death, in a hospital, was caused by non-small-cell lung cancer, her brother Tirso Fernández Jr. said.

An associate professor of history at Baruch College, Dr. Fernández was unaware of the Young Lords until her junior year at Brown, when she took a class that covered the radical group and was angered that it had been effectively erased from public memory.

“I’d say that the children of migrants — especially from Latin America — connect more than anyone else with the history of the Young Lords,” she said in a 2020 interview with CounterPunch, a left-leaning website. “Because you wake up and all you see is death and abandoned buildings and you start believing what people and the media say about you.”

She added, “Then to see your own people take it and shred it and fight it in the streets — that’s freedom on a profound personal level.”

The Young Lords started as a street gang in Chicago and expanded to New York City in 1969. They were a confrontational, anticapitalist collective of Hispanic — mostly Puerto Rican — and Black activists who sought solutions to the deplorable conditions of neighborhoods like the South Bronx and Spanish Harlem.

To protest poor trash collection, they built walls of garbage across city streets, then set the walls on fire. They commandeered a church and used it to offer free breakfast to schoolchildren. They occupied a building at the dilapidated Lincoln Hospital in the Bronx, placed a Puerto Rican flag on the roof and made demands that included building a new hospital, door-to-door preventive care and opening a day care center for the children of patients and employees.

The group’s history was the subject of Dr. Fernández’s Ph.D. dissertation at Columbia, which she completed in 2004 and later expanded into a book.

“She interviewed me three times over 15 years,” the journalist Juan González, a founder of the group’s New York branch, said in an interview. “At first, she didn’t know a lot, but she was determined to speak to everyone. She spoke to a lot of people who weren’t speaking to each other because of past conflicts.”

Her research was impeded by the supposed inaccessibility of extensive surveillance files, more than 500 boxes’ worth, that had been accumulated by the New York Police Department’s secretive special services division from 1954 to 1972. She was told the files were missing or lost.

In 2014, after her Freedom of Information Law requests yielded little, she filed a lawsuit against the N.Y.P.D. seeking the documents. The suit was dismissed but, in 2016, a significant portion of the records of the department’s scrutiny of the Young Lords, the Black Panthers and the Nation of Islam resurfaced during an inventory of a Queens warehouse.

The files told the story of “thousands of people and organizations in New York City who fought to make the city more just and democratic and were systematically obstructed by the police,” Dr. Fernández said in a 2016 interview with The New York Times.

She used information gleaned from the files in her book “The Young Lords: A Radical History” (2020).

In his review in The Nation, Ed Morales, an expert on Latino politics, wrote that the book placed the Young Lords “in the context of the political and social debates that shaped the era and reveals how so much of their activism centered on the same issues — housing, health, education and the marginalization of women, the L.G.B.T.Q. community and the working poor — that we face today.”

“The Young Lords” won the 2021 Frederick Jackson Turner Award from the Organization of American Historians.

Johanna Luisa del Carmen Fernández was born in Manhattan on Dec. 2, 1970, and grew up in the Bronx. She was one of four children of Tirso Sr. and Minerva (Estevez) Fernández, immigrants from the Dominican Republic. Mr. Fernández was a maintenance worker, and Mrs. Fernández managed the home.

Dr. Fernández’s brother Tirso Jr. said their father “had been orphaned as a child and knew real hunger, but it didn’t harden him. Instead, it made him deeply compassionate.”

“Johanna took that and ran with it,” he added. “Her own intellect took her the rest of the way, into history, race, class, power.”

In addition to Tirso Jr., she is survived by her mother and two other brothers, Osvaldo and Geovanny.

In 1992, while attending Brown on an academic scholarship, Dr. Fernández was one of 253 students arrested for taking over an administration building; their demands included a need-blind admission policy. At one point, she attracted a crowd by delivering a speech from the open window of a bathroom. Need-blind admissions at Brown did not start until 2003.

She graduated in 1992 with a bachelor’s degree in English and American civilization, then earned an M.A. in 1996, an M.Phil. in 1999 and a Ph.D. in 2004, all in history from Columbia.

As a postdoctoral fellow at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh from 2005 to 2006, she grew interested in prison abolition and the case of Mumia Abu-Jamal, a former Black Panther and radio journalist then on death row after being convicted of murdering a white police officer in Philadelphia in 1981. To his supporters, Mr. Abu-Jamal is a political prisoner who should be released. To his critics, he is a celebrity cop killer.

Dr. Fernández told CounterPunch that visiting Mr. Abu-Jamal and other men on death row “transformed me, because you get a sense of a whole country of human beings who’ve been thrown away.”

She became close to Mr. Abu-Jamal. She wrote and produced “Justice on Trial: The Case of Mumia Abu-Jamal” (2010), a documentary about his case; edited a book of his prison writings that was published in 2015; and brought a trove of his papers to a permanent archive at Brown in 2024.

In 2012, a year after Mr. Abu-Jamal left death row — he is now serving a life sentence without the possibility of parole — Dr. Fernández began storing boxes of his materials in her apartment. “They were pressuring him to get rid of everything in his cell,” she told The Times. “He wanted to throw it all away. But as a historian, I understood the importance of papers.”

Mr. Abu-Jamal spoke by phone at Dr. Fernández’s funeral on Sunday, calling her “a shock of light in the darkness of death row,” according to her brother.

In 2015, she was a curator of “¡Presente! The Young Lords in New York,” an exhibition that was presented at El Museo del Barrio, the Bronx Museum and the Loisaida Inc. community center and showed the group as a cultural and political force.

An exhibition about the Latino civil rights movement of the 1960s — which Dr. Fernández organized with Felipe Hinojosa of Baylor University — was scheduled to open last year in Washington under the auspices of the Smithsonian Institution. But it was shelved after conservative commentators and members of Congress criticized a previous Smithsonian show about Latino history as Marxist.

With a grant from the Mellon Foundation, the project was revived in June at the Shed in Manhattan as an outdoor exhibition called “Latinx Freedom” that will be on display through Aug. 16 before touring to several American cities.

“She was such a joy — a relentless hard worker who was never satisfied with one answer,” Dr. Hinojosa said in an interview. “She took great offense at the kind of anti-Latino sentiment that exists in this country and worked as hard as she could to make people understand the gifts that Latinos bring to the United States.”

item.title: Woman Arrested After Confessing to Starting Nevada Fire, Officials Say
item.description:
A woman was arrested after she told firefighters that she had intentionally set fires that became part of a larger blaze that is still burning along the border of California and Nevada, the authorities said Tuesday.

The woman, Christine Mitchell, 47, was arrested on suspicion of third-degree arson and possession of less than 14 grams of a controlled substance, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office in Nevada said in a statement on Tuesday. Ms. Mitchell’s public defender didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Mitchell left a home near Freds Mountain Road and set multiple fires, the sheriff’s office said. She caught the attention of firefighters who were responding to the resulting blaze, known as the Fred Mountain fire, and told them she had meant to start the fire.

The Fred Mountain fire, which is burning north of Reno, Nev., has since merged with another nearby wildfire, known as the Bug fire. The Bug fire has covered more than 70,000 acres and has forced thousands of people to evacuate, including from tribal land. It’s one of many large wildfires burning in the western United States during a fire season that has been unusually active for much of the region.

Ms. Mitchell was taken into custody on Sunday. Senior Judge Derek Dreiling at the Reno Justice Court set her bail at $80,000 on Tuesday, according to court records.

The sheriff’s office did not explain what the authorities believed Ms. Mitchell’s motive might have been for starting the fires.

The Reno-Sparks Indian Colony declared an emergency in response to the fires, and its Hungry Valley community was evacuated. Another large blaze east of the Bug fire, called the Stallion fire, is threatening Pyramid Lake Paiute tribal land. The Stallion fire, which officials said was caused by a human, was not contained as of Wednesday morning.

“We understand our Hungry Valley residents are frustrated,” Bethany Sam, a spokeswoman for Reno-Sparks Indian Colony, said during a Facebook livestream Tuesday night. “We know you all want to come home, check on your property, take care of your animals and get back to your normal lives.”

Gov. Joe Lombardo of Nevada also declared a state of emergency on Monday, citing a shortage of wildland fire resources as several wildfires burned across the region.

This week, the Federal Emergency Management Agency authorized the use of federal funds to help Nevada fight the fires.

item.title: ICE Agent Who Pushed Activist to the Ground Pleads Guilty
item.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor battery charge on Wednesday for throwing an activist to the ground near Chicago last year during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in the region.

A judge in Cook County, Ill., sentenced the agent, Adam Saracco, to 12 months of supervision on Wednesday and ordered him not to have contact with the activist he had clashed with, Robert Held.

Mr. Saracco, 41, was charged with misdemeanor battery earlier this year after the altercation in December. At a gas station in Brookfield, Ill., Mr. Held was filming Mr. Saracco when Mr. Saracco approached him. Mr. Saracco took Mr. Held’s phone and threw him to the ground. Mr. Saracco was off duty at the time and was getting gas after leaving a nearby immigration detention center. Mr. Held said he did not sustain any injuries.

It was not clear whether Mr. Saracco was still employed by ICE. Neither Mr. Saracco nor the Department of Homeland Security responded to requests for comment on Wednesday.

Mr. Held, a trust and estate lawyer, joined many Illinois residents in protesting against ICE last fall amid a surge in immigration arrests across the Chicago area, which the Trump administration called Operation Midway Blitz.

“I am pleased that there is some accountability,” Mr. Held, 68, said in an interview on Wednesday. He added that he remained “deeply troubled and concerned” by the actions of federal agents.

“This resolution represents an important step for accountability and shows that Cook County will not turn a blind eye to unlawful conduct, no matter who you are,” Eileen O’Neill Burke, the state’s attorney for Cook County, said in a statement on Wednesday.

Ms. Burke said that her office would seek justice on behalf of those harmed during the Trump administration’s crackdown in the Chicago area “when the evidence and the law allow us to prosecute.” There have been very few local prosecutions of immigration agents.

item.title: A Fight Over Abortion and Surrogacy Ends With a Baby Born in Texas
item.description:
A bitter confrontation over surrogacy, abortion and parental rights that stretched across three states culminated on Wednesday with the birth of the baby at the center of the conflict at a Dallas hospital.

The fate of the baby, who has a severe birth defect, became a cause this summer among anti-abortion activists, who provided legal representation for the surrogate, McKenna West, and helped her travel to Texas for medical care. This week, she also received support from the Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton, who took legal action to compel medical treatments for the newborn.

The dispute began in the spring after the discovery at around 20 weeks of pregnancy that the fetus had a rare and life-threatening congenital heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, and would require multiple surgeries to survive.

The intended parents, who live in Los Angeles, opted to terminate the pregnancy.

But Ms. West, who lives in Alaska, refused to have an abortion. Instead, she went to Texas, which bans abortion, to seek specialists who could treat the baby’s defect.

On Wednesday, amid overlapping legal actions in the three states, Ms. West gave birth to a boy in Dallas whom activists have called “Baby Gabriel.” His legal parents, Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar, chose a different name.

“As if the heartbreak of his condition were not enough, they are devastated to see their family tragedy transformed into political theater by the Texas Attorney General’s office and McKenna West,” said a lawyer for the parents, Lee Budner, in a statement.

Mr. Budner said the boy was “now receiving medical care provided by a team of pediatric experts,” adding that the parents “would place their baby’s health and well-being first, following the advice of the baby’s medical team.”

Ms. West is seeking custody of the child.

The birth came just days after Mr. Paxton’s legal intervention on Monday. Mr. Paxton, a Republican locked in a tough race for the U.S. Senate, argued in Dallas County court that the parents were required to provide lifesaving care under Texas law.

“My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives,” Mr. Paxton said in a statement.

The move sharply increased attention on what had already been a cause célèbre in anti-abortion circles this summer.

By Tuesday, Mr. Paxton celebrated having secured a temporary restraining order, or T.R.O., in Dallas that prevents the parents from removing the child from Texas until a hearing in late August. The order also requires them to provide “medically indicated, lifesaving treatment” to the baby.

At the same time, the Dallas County court also issued another restraining order against Ms. West. The order bars Ms. West from presenting herself as the baby’s parent, guardian or medical-decision maker “to anyone.”

“Unfortunately, because of the Texas T.R.O. that was entered yesterday, McKenna didn’t get to see or hold him after he was born,” Lincoln Wilson, a lawyer for Ms. West, said in an interview.

Ms. West, who did not respond to an interview request for this story, said in an interview this month with the former Fox News and current YouTube host Megyn Kelly that she did not support abortion and felt “trapped” by the surrogacy contract, which permitted the intended parents to end the pregnancy via abortion.

“It brought up a lot of fear,” said Ms. West, a nurse with two children of her own, in the interview.

Through a mutual friend, Ms. West connected with Lila Rose, the president of Live Action, an anti-abortion group. Ms. Rose said she helped Ms. West get legal support from the Alliance Defending Freedom, a prominent Christian conservative legal organization.

“There came a point where she, for the sake of her own medical care and safety, needed to travel to Texas, and so we did assist,” Ms. Rose said. “They were treating her baby like a product. The product had a defect, and so they were trying to send it back.”

Ms. Rose said that her organization does not support surrogacy, which “commoditizes human life” and leads to “heartbreaking and devastating situations like this.”

Mr. Wilson, the lawyer for Ms. West, said that the legal case was not over and that Ms. West would continue to fight for custody of the boy, who must undergo weeks of surgeries “before he’s really in the clear.”

item.title: The Debate Over Democrats’ Future Rages On After Hong’s Defeat in Wisconsin
item.description:
Francesca Hong was supposed to prove that a democratic socialist could win a statewide election.

Instead, her surprise loss in the primary election for governor of Wisconsin dealt a blow to the progressive movement and initiated a scramble among Democratic factions to define her narrow defeat either as an impressive harbinger of the movement’s future or an ominous sign of voter antipathy toward the far left.

Some prominent Democrats argued that the outcome was proof that the moderate wing of the party carried more electoral weight than the progressive one, which has dominated headlines this year as insurgent candidates have ousted incumbents in deep-blue cities.

Others, on the left, looked to celebrate the tight race — even though their candidate fell short — as evidence that progressives can compete in statewide contests.

“It’s a significant loss,” Robert Lasica, a spokesman for Madison’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter, said in an interview. But he argued the race was also “a big triumph of how far we can go with building the left infrastructure in Wisconsin that simply did not exist a year ago.”

David Crowley, who is the Milwaukee County executive and had briefly suspended his campaign just over a month ago, defeated Ms. Hong by a razor-thin margin. His victory defied months of polls that showed Ms. Hong far in the lead.

It was the second consecutive week with a Democratic primary in which a progressive candidate underperformed expectations. Last week in the Democratic Senate race in Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Representative Haley Stevens, but the contest was closer than expected and was not called until the next morning. Both narrow outcomes have kept the debate that has been raging all year between moderates and progressives vigorously alive.

Mr. El-Sayed is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, and the D.S.A. is not officially part of the Democratic Party. But both the D.S.A. and non-D.S.A. progressives have roiled the party in this year’s midterms by exciting the left flank of the party’s base.

Some in the party hoped to export aspects of Ms. Hong’s success to other campaigns, notably her ground game. The former chef and restaurateur spent more time than any other candidate campaigning in rural Wisconsin, and it appeared to pay off with strong margins in some of those counties. Progressives have won a string of races partly on the strength of their ground games. The question is whether the model can be replicated without the populist policy proposals, such as abolishing I.C.E., that are resonating with some voters but that many moderates eschew.

The fallout of Ms. Hong’s campaign carries extra weight as the party eyes 2028, with those in each wing already jockeying to elevate their own. On Wednesday, Democrats openly exploring presidential bids sought to wield the election results to make their cases.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and former chief of staff to President Barack Obama, wrote on social media that Ms. Hong’s defeat showed “that the pragmatic wing isn’t a faction of this party. It’s the majority, it’s awake now, and it’s exerting itself.”

Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive congressman from California who had endorsed Ms. Hong and is also contemplating a run for president, sought to tamp down criticism of the far left.

“I appreciate that Democrats can have differences over single payer healthcare, free childcare, pausing data centers and other issues @FrancescaHongWI fought for,” he wrote on X. “But caricaturing and labeling candidates based on a few statements is not a politics I believe in.”

Democratic socialists had seen Wisconsin as a key opportunity to prove that their message could resonate in less liberal parts of the country. While they planned to study Ms. Hong’s loss to improve their electoral fortunes, several said they viewed Tuesday’s result as strong proof of the movement’s rise.

“Francesa won hundreds of thousands of votes — one of the highest vote totals of a democratic socialist candidate in any election in the United States,” said Katie Sims, a D.S.A. member in Ithaca, N.Y., who leads the group’s national electoral strategy. “Ultimately, it’s disappointing that she lost by such a small margin, but really heartening that it shows that these kinds of races are viable.”

D.S.A. members pointed to several areas for improvement. For one, the socialist infrastructure and campaign experience in Wisconsin was far less robust than in places such as New York City, which last fall elected Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, to be mayor. There, socialists had been building for years toward that victory as well as additional successes in congressional campaigns in June.

“For some people on the campaign, they have not worked at this scale yet before under these pressures,” Mr. Lasica said. “Next time around, we’re going to be in a better position.”

Some progressives criticized some of the biggest national names in their movement, including Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, for sitting out the race.

Ms. Hong also struggled in the final days of her campaign to explain past online remarks that were unearthed in news reports — including one in which she suggested canceling Thanksgiving.

Those reports unfurled an examination on the left, too, of how positions and rhetoric of pandemic-era progressivism have not always aged well with the broader population. Ms. Ocasio-Cortez jumped into that debate on ABC’s “This Week” on Sunday, describing that era as “crazy” and “Woke 1.0” — a term that has become a political meme.

Asked about those comments on Wednesday and whether “Woke 1.0” was indeed crazy, Mr. Mamdani stressed that elected officials have a responsibility to own their evolving beliefs.

“I think that each person has a responsibility to tell New Yorkers, to tell Americans, when they’re running for office what they believe,” he said to reporters. “And sometimes what you believe can change, it can develop, it can grow.”

Dana Rubinstein and Tim Balk contributed reporting.

item.title: Federal Hate Crime Charge Filed in Stabbing of Muslim Man in Utah
item.description:
A man in Utah was indicted on a federal hate crime charge after he rode a scooter to a mall, bought a knife and repeatedly stabbed a Muslim man selling wares at a kiosk, the authorities said on Wednesday.

Federal prosecutors in Salt Lake City said Peter Larsen, 48, was indicted in connection with a stabbing on July 13 at the mall, in West Valley City. The victim was stabbed about a dozen times, on his head, chest and arms, causing internal bleeding, the authorities said, and a man who tried to intervene was also stabbed.

Mr. Larsen also faced state charges, including two counts of attempted aggravated murder and one count of having a dangerous weapon, according to the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. It was not immediately clear what would happen with the state charges as the federal case proceeded.

“An alleged unprovoked attack on anyone in our community is unacceptable, but an attack allegedly motivated because of the victim’s religion is alarming,” the Salt Lake County district attorney, Sim Gill, said in a statement announcing the state charges.

Mr. Gill did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It was not clear whether Mr. Larsen had a lawyer. Mr. Larsen faces life in prison on the federal count, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The attack began when Mr. Larsen approached the victim and asked for water, according to a charging document filed by the Salt Lake County District Attorney’s Office. The authorities have said the ordeal was captured on the mall’s surveillance video and on witnesses’ cellphones.

Mr. Larsen asked the victim if he was Muslim, and after hearing that he was, Mr. Larsen said, “Everything is like Jesus Christ,” prosecutors said. He then began stabbing the man with a knife he had bought earlier that day, they said.

Several witnesses rushed toward Mr. Larsen and tried to subdue him. One person punched Mr. Larsen repeatedly, knocking him out, prosecutors said.

Another witness said he heard the victim calling for God and his mother.

Mr. Larsen told the authorities that he had planned to arrive at the mall and make an “exhibition of Muslims and hopefully be a catalyst so people would rid the country of Muslims,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Larsen also may have communicated with other people who shared his anti-Muslim beliefs, his brother told the authorities, according to prosecutors.

Witnesses told the authorities that Mr. Larsen approached other brown-skinned people in the mall and questioned their ethnicity and religious beliefs. The individuals who identified as Muslim worked behind a counter, rendering them inaccessible to Mr. Larsen, prosecutors said.

“Unfortunately for victim, he was working at a kiosk completely exposed and accessible,” they said.

Mr. Larsen will appear in court on Thursday in Salt Lake City. He has previous convictions of assaulting a police officer, arson and driving under the influence, prosecutors said.

item.title: Trump Administration Lets Key Gun Law Lapse Following Court Ruling
item.description:
The Justice Department declined to appeal a court ruling that effectively dismantled longstanding restrictions on owning short-barreled guns and suppressors, bowing to pressure from Republicans and gun advocates.

Judge James Wesley Hendrix of the Northern District of Texas had said that his order striking down the mandated permitting process under the National Firearms Act as unconstitutional would go into effect Thursday unless the Justice Department appealed it. Trump administration officials didn’t file an appeal to the court before 12:01 a.m. Thursday, according to publicly available court records.

In effect, the Trump administration stepped aside, for now, and allowed the Prohibition-era gun control measure to lapse under judicial scrutiny after President Trump signed a law last year that weakened the restrictions by removing a $200 tax for the permit. The administration has another 52 days to file an appeal in the case.

Gun rights groups and gun businesses, many of which had filed and supported the lawsuit, celebrated the overturning of the law. Groups supporting gun restrictions criticized the government’s inaction, arguing that the ruling had deregulated dangerous, easily concealable firearms and accessories that had been restricted since 1934.

The Justice Department did not explain why it did not immediately appeal the ruling. In an unsigned statement to The New York Times hours before the midnight deadline, the Justice Department said that it “respects Americans’ Second Amendment rights and is currently assessing the impact of the court’s ruling.”

It was a retreat by the Trump administration, which had argued after Mr. Trump’s law was passed last year that Congress still had the authority to restrict particularly dangerous and easily concealable weapons. The government’s move to forgo a stay of the ruling — or issue any public statement on the issue — came after gun rights groups and dozens of Republican lawmakers publicly pressured Todd Blanche, the attorney general, to allow the ruling to stand.

“The Department of Justice had the opportunity to act to protect our safety, but it failed to do so,” Kris Brown, the president of the Brady Campaign to Prevent Gun Violence, said in a statement, noting the campaign from Republican lawmakers. “Our elected officials are supposed to serve the American people, not the gun industry’s bottom line. Today, the gun industry and silencer dealers are celebrating, while Americans are left less safe.”

Seeking clarification from the government on where it stood on the ruling, the lobbying group Gun Owners of America issued a public letter Wednesday to Trump administration officials. It said that gun stores planned to start selling suppressors, which are devices fitted onto the barrel of a gun to reduce the deafening sound of gunfire, without following the permitting process after midnight Thursday.

Gun buyers will still need to complete a standard background check to purchase the weapons, and restrictions under state laws will still apply. California, New York and Washington, D.C., for example, have banned the sale and ownership of short-barreled rifles and suppressors.

The National Firearms Act was the primary law that regulated and restricted the sale and possession of suppressors. Once a niche accessory for civilian gun owners, the popularity of suppressors has skyrocketed in recent years, as more gun owners use them to prevent hearing damage and brain injuries.

The effect of Judge Hendrix’s ruling is wide, but not universal. The Supreme Court limited the ability of lower-court judges to completely block executive branch policies nationwide, but the ruling still applies to a wide class of millions of gun owners, as well as retailers and manufacturers. Many states also joined the lawsuit. Crucially, the ruling also applies to customers of the businesses who were part of the case. One of the retailers, Palmetto State Armory, is one of the largest online gun stores in the country.

The National Firearms Act of 1934 had instituted a tax-and-registration requirement for rifles and shotguns with short barrels, as well as for suppressors — weapons that Congress sought to curb because they were deemed particularly suited for violent crime. The law was written as lawmakers warned of a “serious national emergency” driven by gun crime as the country reeled from Prohibition-era gang shootings and an attempted assassination of President-elect Franklin D. Roosevelt.

The law also regulated the sale and ownership of machine guns through the permitting process, but that part of the law remains intact.

Millions of N.F.A. restricted guns and suppressors were sold every year under the registration process, which is managed by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. The $200 tax was designed to be prohibitively expensive in 1934 dollars, but by 2026 amounted to a fraction of the cost of a modern firearm or suppressor.

House Republicans added a provision eliminating the $200 tax on suppressors and short-barreled rifles when they passed Mr. Trump’s major spending bill last year.

That change triggered the downfall of the law, which had for 92 years required buyers of restricted arms to submit their fingerprints and seek A.T.F. approval. Gun advocacy groups quickly filed several lawsuits seeking to further weaken the law, arguing that the registration process was unconstitutional without the tax component.

Judge Hendrix agreed with that argument, ruling in a 66-page order that because the law no longer generated revenue, “its regulatory provisions cannot be upheld under the taxing power” given to Congress in Article 1 of the Constitution.

item.title: In This State, an Intense Fight in the G.O.P. for Control of the Right
item.description:
Wyoming, one of the most conservative states, has a legislature divided between a hard-right House and a merely right Senate. Ultraconservatives want a complete takeover in the Aug. 18 primaries.

By David W. Chen

Photographs by Will Warasila

David W. Chen and Will Warasila reported from Senate District 1 in northeastern Wyoming, bordering South Dakota and Montana.

In the shadow of Devils Tower, the national monument immortalized by Steven Spielberg’s “Close Encounters of the Third Kind,” an election-year fight has erupted between Wyoming’s right and its far right, with serious implications for the state’s political future.

On the far right is State Representative Chip Neiman, the House speaker and a member of Wyoming’s ultraconservative Freedom Caucus, the country’s first such caucus to control a statehouse chamber. On the merely right is State Senator Ogden Driskill, whose chamber has often thwarted the Freedom Caucus agenda.

In an unusual gamble, Mr. Neiman is giving up his speaker’s gavel to take on Mr. Driskill, a former State Senate president, in the Aug. 18 Republican primary.

“Challenging the status quo — I think it’s critical,” Mr. Neiman said at his cattle ranch in Hulett, Wyo. “We need to move more conservatives to the Senate.”

With U.S. Senator Cynthia Lummis declining to seek re-election, Harriet Hageman, a hard-core conservative, vacating the state’s lone U.S. House seat to run for Senate, and Gov. Mark Gordon facing term limits, Wyoming voters face a choice, from the statehouse to the governor’s mansion to the U.S. Capitol. They can expand — or check — ultraconservative power.

The schism echoes struggles between institutionalists and insurgents elsewhere, especially among Democrats, but it feels especially personal in Wyoming. The nation’s least populous state has produced national figures, Dick and Liz Cheney, the now-deceased Senator Alan K. Simpson and the current Senate majority whip, John Barrasso. It has also attracted an influx of billionaires, heightening class anger and affordability issues.

If hard-right candidates triumph, some groups such as Common Sense Republicans warn of deep cuts to schools, towns and law enforcement. Americans for Prosperity, a veteran conservative group that targeted moderate Montana Republican legislators this year, is now championing more than a dozen non-Freedom Caucus legislative candidates, Mr. Driskill included.

Freedom Caucus legislators “weren’t willing to work with others to find a solution,” said Tyler Lindholm, the Wyoming state director of Americans for Prosperity and a former state representative who lost to Mr. Neiman in the 2020 primary.

The first plank of the Wyoming Republican Party’s 23-plank platform, trumpeted by the Freedom Caucus, declares that life begins at conception. Others highlight the role of faith and biblical principles in the nation’s founding and the “freedom” to decline childhood vaccines.

Campaign signs on ranches and roads tout “platform Republican” candidates, but Mr. Driskill dismissed what he called a platform “purity test.”

This year, Mr. Driskill, 67, helped block attempts to slash funding to the University of Wyoming and gut the state’s economic development office. Elected in 2010, he planned to retire at year’s end to the family’s Campstool Ranch at the foot of Devils Tower, where his father shook hands with Mr. Spielberg 50 years ago.

But when Mr. Neiman, who lives five miles down the highway, sought to succeed him, Mr. Driskill decided to fight.

“I hate the Freedom Caucus and how they do business,” he said.

Mr. Neiman, 59, says Mr. Driskill has “Freedom Caucus derangement syndrome.”

Elected in 2020, Mr. Neiman pushed to make Wyoming the first state to ban abortion pills, a law struck down by the State Supreme Court. He supported a program that offers $7,000-per-student vouchers to pay private school tuition. He criticized the State Senate for failing to ban what he called sexually explicit books from libraries and schools.

“I don’t know what the Lord’s plan is, but I’m glad to just let Him order my steps,” he said, pounding in campaign signs with his son Preston on Highway 14.

Future priorities include shrinking government, tightening voting rules and curtailing “activist” judges, said State Representative Rachel Williams, the Freedom Caucus chairwoman, who is running for secretary of state.

“The left tends to be very loud in Wyoming,” she said, “and our supporters tend to be the silent majority.”

Early voting started on July 21. In Sundance, Wyo., where signs warn “Do Not Jackson Hole My Sundance,” Amy Goodson, executive director of the Crook County Museum District, said Mr. Driskill helped save a historic school by turning it into a cultural center.

“Every roadblock they put in front of him, he said, ‘That’s not a ‘no,’ that’s a ‘what else can you do?’” she said.

At Wyoming’s oldest general store in Aladdin, near the South Dakota border, Jordan Yates, a co-owner, likes that the Driskills protected 5,000 acres surrounding Devils Tower from future development.

But Trent Tope, her fiancé and co-owner, said Mr. Neiman is more approachable; he has been to the store, goes to churches and shows up to pie socials.

“Even though I don’t agree with everything, at least I can speak to the man and not feel like a peasant,” he said.

Hello everyone. Two years ago, I traveled to Wyoming to report on the rise of the Freedom Caucus, which had become the first in the country to take control of a statehouse chamber. So when I heard from sources earlier this year that the House Speaker, a Freedom Caucus member, was giving up his gavel in order to challenge a longtime Senator in this year's midterms -- a fellow cattle rancher who lives just five miles away, and is hardly a moderate -- I was intrigued. Here is what I found, and what made the final cut.

item.title: Homeland Security Paid $464 Million for Airplanes. Then It Parked Them.
item.description:
Starting last fall, the Department of Homeland Security spent $464 million on a no-bid contract to buy 10 used airplanes from a firm in Northern Virginia.

That was an enormous price tag, but the department said it had no time to consider other offers. The planes were needed urgently for deportation flights.

But since then, the department has barely used this new fleet — for deportations, or anything else.

Three of the aircraft are luxury business jets. Just months after acquiring them, the department sought to loan or lease two to other agencies, including one for the use of F.B.I. director Kash Patel, according to a letter to the department sent Wednesday by top Democrats on the Senate Appropriations Committee.

The other seven are older Boeing 737 passenger jets, which the government has left parked at an airport in Lake Charles, La., for months at a time. An internal government document, obtained by The New York Times, said the agency did not have the staff necessary to operate them.

The acquisitions were part of a surge of rushed contracts handed out recently by the Homeland Security Department, which has repeatedly used the need for “urgency” to bypass regular contracting procedures. The idled planes highlight the risks of that approach. The agency rushed headlong to spend nearly half a billion dollars, only to end up with planes it did not fly.

The contract also illuminated a broader trend within the second Trump administration: no-bid contracts awarded to people with connections to Mr. Trump or his cabinet secretaries. The company that received this contract, Daedalus Aviation Corporation, is led by a chairman who had donated to a political committee supporting the previous Homeland Security Secretary, Kristi Noem.

The department’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency has long outsourced its deportation flights by chartering planes from private companies. It also uses military and Coast Guard aircraft. Because of that, former immigration officials said there seemed to be little need for the department to take on the expense of buying and maintaining a significant number of its own aircraft.

“If you asked me to write a list of the things ICE needed to increase the number of deportations, buying its own fleet of airplanes would absolutely not make the top ten,” said John Sandweg, a former acting director of ICE during the Obama administration.

In a written statement, the Homeland Security Department sought to shift responsibility for the contract to Ms. Noem. President Trump fired her in March, and appointed Markwayne Mullin, a Republican Senator from Oklahoma, as secretary.

“The contract for Daedalus was made and approved by department leadership before Secretary Mullin was sworn in,” the department said in a statement. The agency said it “reserves the right to adjust course in an environment with evolving requirements and demands.”

A spokeswoman for Ms. Noem sought to place the responsibility on Mr. Mullin instead, saying the purchase was “finalized” under his leadership.

Contracting records show that the size of the contract increased by $303 million on the day that Mr. Mullin was sworn in as secretary.

The agency said that the idle 737 passenger jets had been undergoing maintenance checks, and that there were plans for two of them to begin deportation flights later this month.

The situation with the planes was reminiscent of the department’s about-face on a plan to acquire warehouses to hold detainees. The department spent heavily on those when Ms. Noem was secretary, but reversed itself just months later under Mr. Mullin. The department is now giving away or selling seven warehouses that it bought for more than $700 million.

A letter sent to the department Wednesday by Democratic senators Patty Murray of Washington and Christopher Murphy of Connecticut, who sit on the Senate Appropriations Committee, said Homeland Security officials had already conceded to the committee that most of the planes would not be used for deportations.

“The American people deserve a full accounting of this gross misuse of their tax dollars,” the letter, which was reviewed by The Times, said.

The senators asked for details about the purchase price of each plane and how they would be used.

Federal law generally requires government agencies to seek competing bids before awarding a contract, to ensure taxpayers get the best deal. But the department sidestepped that requirement for the planes contract, by invoking an exemption for cases of “unusual and compelling urgency.”

That exemption can be used only when delaying the contract would result in “serious injury, financial or other,” to the government. Historically, it has been used during natural disasters, war and the coronavirus pandemic.

The department declined to answer questions about what serious injury it was trying to prevent. Contracting regulations require agencies to publish the rationales for no-bid contracts, but the department refused to release this one, saying it “would compromise national security or create other security risks.”

Got a confidential news tip? The New York Times would like to hear from readers who want to share messages and materials with our journalists.

The department has invoked the urgency exemption to justify more than $29 billion in spending across about 500 contracts awarded during Mr. Trump’s second term, according to an analysis of federal data by The Times. Much of that total came from border wall spending. Urgency claims were also used to justify projects like the $220 million in media contracts awarded to firms tied to Ms. Noem and her allies, scrutiny over which contributed to her ouster.

The exemption accounts for nearly two-thirds of the $34 billion that the department has spent on contracts signed in 2026. That’s up sharply from past years. In 2025, the figure was about one-quarter. In 2024, it was less than 1 percent.

Department of Homeland Security spending on contracts, by year signed

Note: Years reflect the dates contracts were originally signed, even if payouts occurred later. Data through Aug. 4, 2026.

Source: USAspending.gov.

The New York Times

No other major agency has used the exemption for urgency as frequently as Homeland Security, even in an administration that has turned to no-bid contracts repeatedly — for event planning, fountain repair and the troubled makeover of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.

Lorna Tedder, a retired contracting expert who spent more than three decades at the Defense Department, said that, “Some things truly are urgent — people are going to die if you don’t do this.” But if agencies claim the exemption all the time, “it will eventually be abused.”

The contract for the planes was first awarded in late November. At the time, the government was already paying other contractors hundreds of millions to operate a network of charter flights called “ICE Air.”

The immigration agency has chartered about 25,800 flights in Mr. Trump’s second term, shuttling immigrants between detention centers domestically and deporting them abroad, mainly to Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the ICE Flight Monitor tracking project at Human Rights First, a nonprofit advocacy group. The department sometimes has 25 or more planes in the air in a day, according to the nonprofit’s tracking.

But at the time, the Homeland Security Department said it still needed its own planes.

Last fall, Tricia McLaughlin, a department spokeswoman, told The Washington Post that purchasing the planes would allow “ICE to operate more effectively, including by using more efficient flight patterns.” Ms. McLaughlin has since left the agency. The department did not respond directly to a question asking about her comments.

Daedalus, the Arlington, Va.-based company the government hired to find the planes, had not previously held a federal contract. However, a company spokesman said it had worked as a subcontractor to other companies evacuating Afghans who had done work for the U.S. government.

Daedalus’s chairman is William Walters, a doctor who until 2021 led a State Department office that evacuated Americans from outbreaks of Ebola, Covid-19 and other crises. In 2024, after leaving government, Mr. Walters donated $10,000 to a political committee connected to Ms. Noem, then the governor of South Dakota.

Last year, with Ms. Noem in charge, the agency gave a separate company run by Mr. Walters a contract worth nearly $700 million to encourage immigrants to leave the U.S. voluntarily.

A Daedalus spokesman said that Mr. Walters was unaware that the political committee was tied to Ms. Noem.

Daedalus declined to say how much each of the 10 planes had cost, or what its profit margin was for acting, essentially, as a broker. It provided a written statement that it was proud to provide “the best value to the American taxpayer.”

One of the planes is a Boeing 737 luxury jet, now painted in the color scheme of Mr. Trump’s new Air Force One. Two others are smaller Gulfstream business jets, each seating about 14 people.

Those planes flew only sporadically after the agency acquired them, according to flight records from airplanes.live, an independent flight tracking service. And the department soon moved to jettison two of them to other agencies, according to the account from Senate Democrats and the internal document reviewed by The Times.

One of the luxury jets “has already been leased to the F.B.I. for 12 months to support director Patel’s travel — despite the fact that the F.B.I. already has its own jets to support the director’s travel,” the Senate Democrats wrote.

The F.B.I. confirmed that it is using one of the Gulfstream jets, saying it was paying the Homeland Security Department significantly less than it had paid a private company to lease a similar plane and that the aircraft was being used to support a range of agency operations, in addition to Mr. Patel’s travel.

The Homeland Security Department also wanted to lend the larger Boeing luxury jet to the Pentagon, according to the senators’ letter and the internal document. But a Pentagon spokesman said no agreement had been signed.

One Gulfstream jet will remain with Homeland Security, for the use of its top leaders, according to the letter.

The other 737s seemed more suited for deportation flights. Flight records show they had been in active use by Avelo Airlines, a low-cost carrier that also flew charter flights for ICE.

But when the government bought them, it parked them.

Daedalus said that two were used briefly to evacuate Americans from the Middle East at the outbreak of the Iran War in early March.

Senate Democrats said they were told by Homeland Security staff that four of the 737s were no longer expected to fly detained immigrants. The senators said the department said it would use them to fly members of Congress on overseas trips, a job now handled by commercial carriers or military aircraft.

For the long term, the agency said it needs a contractor to provide crews and mechanics to operate its new fleet. A recent solicitation said that contract would start next summer.

Devlin Barrett and Madeleine Ngo contributed reporting. Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: Three States to Execute Inmates on the Same Day
item.description:
Three states plan to execute inmates Thursday, in what would be the first time in more than a decade that three people on death row are killed on the same day.

The executions are set to be carried out by lethal injection in Alabama, Oklahoma and Tennessee.

Nationally, states are on track to execute far fewer people in 2026 than in previous years. Public support for capital punishment is at its lowest level in decades, according to Gallup polls, even as the Trump administration has called the death penalty an “essential tool for deterring and punishing” horrific crimes.

Each of the three men scheduled to die Thursday was convicted of murder. In Tennessee, Anthony Darrell Hines, 66, was convicted of the 1985 stabbing and murder of a motel maid. In Oklahoma, Carlos Cuesta-Rodriguez, 70, was convicted of fatally shooting his then-girlfriend in 2003. In Alabama, Jeremy Williams, 42, pleaded guilty to the sexual assault and murder of a 5-year-old girl in 2021.

The planned execution in Tennessee comes after officials called off the scheduled lethal injection in May of Tony Carruthers, a man convicted of three 1993 murders, when medical staff were unable to find a vein. Mr. Carruthers received a yearlong reprieve from Gov. Bill Lee.

Maria DeLiberato, a lawyer for Mr. Carruthers who witnessed the series of failed attempts to insert a line for the lethal drug, later wrote in The New York Times that it was an agonizing experience that lasted more than an hour.

Mr. Hines’s lawyers have asserted that the state’s lethal injection procedure could violate the U.S. Constitution’s prohibition of cruel and unusual punishment. In one court filing, the state of Tennessee responded that “the U.S. and Tennessee Constitutions do not demand avoidance of all pain in executions.”

Mr. Hines was found guilty in 1986 of the stabbing death of Catherine Jenkins at the Kingston Springs motel where she had worked as a maid. He has maintained his innocence and unsuccessfully fought for a new trial in Tennessee.

Tennessee restarted executions in 2025 after a pause begun in 2022 when it admitted that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. Mr. Hines is part of a lawsuit challenging the new injection procedure.

Lawyers for Mr. Hines have also criticized state officials for not disclosing more information about the failed execution of Mr. Carruthers. The state also won’t disclose whether the doctor who was unable to administer the lethal drugs to Mr. Carruthers would be tending to Mr. Hines.

Tennessee officials say that state procedure bars the identification of any medical staff involved in an execution.

As of Wednesday evening, the U.S. Supreme Court had not responded to a request from Mr. Hines’s lawyers to intervene.

Only six states have plans to carry out capital punishment this year. Florida remains by far the most aggressive in its use of the death penalty, accounting for 12 of the 19 executions carried out so far this year.

Oklahoma has executed two people this year. Mr. Cuesta-Rodriguez, the inmate scheduled to be executed there, said at a recent hearing that he did not want clemency, according to local reports. Instead, he said he wanted to apologize to the surviving children of Olimpia Fisher, 43, his then-girlfriend. After a string of domestic assaults, he shot and killed her during a confrontation.

In Alabama, Mr. Williams will be the state’s first person executed this year after the Supreme Court issued a rare decision in June blocking the scheduled execution of another inmate by nitrogen gas. Mr. Williams dropped an appeal and effectively requested that the death penalty be carried out.

Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting from Washington.

item.title: Hegseth Is Pressed to Clarify Lawyer’s Role in Promotion Decisions
item.description:
Representative Jason Crow, Democrat of Colorado, pressed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a letter released on Thursday to clarify his earlier statements about whether his personal lawyer influenced key military promotions.

During a hearing in April, Mr. Crow asked whether Timothy Parlatore, a lawyer who has represented Mr. Hegseth and President Trump, was working on behalf of senior military officers being considered for promotions by Mr. Hegseth.

Mr. Hegseth said that Mr. Parlatore, who is also his “special adviser” at the Pentagon and a Navy reservist, had no role in choosing senior military leaders.

“He doesn’t represent anyone,” Mr. Hegseth testified before the House Armed Services Committee. “He’s a legal adviser and always has been.”

Last month, The New York Times reported that Adm. Daryl Caudle, when he was under consideration to be the chief of naval operations, had hired Mr. Parlatore to help him resolve comments he had made to sailors about the Pentagon’s Sexual Assault Prevention and Response program, officials said. Some interpreted Admiral Caudle’s remarks as blaming victims.

Mr. Crow asked Mr. Hegseth in the letter to explain the apparent contradiction between his congressional testimony and the Times report.

“Our military leaders make decisions of life and death nearly every day, and the American people must see that those leaders are chosen with integrity, merit and their safety top of mind,” Mr. Crow said in a statement. “Undermining this process puts our national security at risk. Hegseth must set the record straight before the American people.”

In an interview with The Times on Wednesday, Mr. Parlatore called Mr. Crow’s letter “misguided.”

“The record is clear that Admiral Caudle had already been selected before he and I had ever spoken,” Mr. Parlatore said. “All of the secretary’s answers at the hearing were completely and totally truthful.”

As part of his work for Admiral Caudle, Mr. Parlatore suggested possible witnesses and accompanied the Naval officer to his interview with investigators.

After the inspector general found the allegations of wrongdoing by Admiral Caudle to be unsubstantiated, his nomination was sent to Mr. Trump for approval.

The Pentagon declined to comment on Mr. Crow’s letter.

In an earlier statement, Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesman, said that all promotion decisions in the Pentagon were based “strictly on merit,” and added that Mr. Parlatore was “in full compliance with all ethics laws and regulations.”

Mr. Hegseth selected Admiral Caudle for the job leading the Navy even though he was not on a list of candidates recommended by senior Navy officials for the position. He took over as the 34th chief of naval operations last summer.

“It appears that Mr. Parlatore’s involvement extended well beyond that of a special adviser and into matters traditionally reserved for department leadership and established military personnel processes,” Mr. Crow wrote in the letter to Mr. Hegseth.

Mr. Parlatore’s involvement in promotion decisions raises “significant questions about potential conflicts of interest, adherence to federal ethics standards, and the integrity and impartiality of the military’s promotion system,” Mr. Crow continued.

He asked Mr. Hegseth to provide a written response clarifying his testimony by Sept. 10.

item.title: How a Covid-Era Scramble Transformed Supreme Court Arguments
item.description:
On about 40 mornings each year, the justices take their seats behind the Supreme Court’s majestic mahogany bench to hear oral arguments.

Part interrogation of the lawyers before them and part conversation among the justices, those sessions are not as important as the written briefs submitted by the parties. But the arguments that follow those submissions are essentially the only way the public can see the court at work.

The ritual had hardly changed in 50 years until the spring of 2020, when the pandemic ousted the justices from the courtroom for 18 months.

Scrambling for a solution, they decided to hold arguments by telephone, revised how they posed questions and let the public listen in.

Those improvised stopgap measures turned out to be the start of a fundamental transformation of the court’s signature ceremony.

When the justices returned to the bench in October 2021, their approach to oral arguments had undergone a revolution. The aftershocks are still reverberating.

The justices allowed live audio of the arguments, letting the public hear what went on in the courtroom in real time from anywhere in the world.

They also revised the format of the arguments, adopting an ungainly hybrid that started with a familiar free-for-all barrage of questions and ended with one-by-one queries in order of the justices’ seniority.

Both developments appear to have prompted lasting consequences.

The length of arguments shot up. Justice Clarence Thomas, who once went a decade without asking a question, became a regular participant. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who joined the court in 2022, quickly became the most talkative member of the court in living memory. Around the same time, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. grew taciturn, rivaling Justice Thomas as the least voluble member of the court.

A comprehensive new study assessed many aspects of this sea change, gathering information on the roughly 16 million words uttered during 1,425 oral arguments from October 2005, just after Chief Justice Roberts joined the court, to April 2026, the most recent time that the court heard arguments.

The study, prepared for The New York Times by Lee Epstein of Washington University in St. Louis and Eric A. Posner of the University of Chicago, revealed momentous changes in a cautious institution. The changes have subjected the court to additional scrutiny, seemed to encourage some justices to talk more and tested the patience of others.

The study examined trends in measurable things like which justices spoke and for how long — it did not try to assess the effectiveness of arguments or whether recent changes had led to more illuminating sessions.

Before the pandemic, arguments lasted an hour. Now they are on average nearly 90 minutes, But that is only an average. In bigger cases, the arguments can seem endless.

The 2024 arguments over presidential immunity and last year’s argument over President Trump’s tariffs program both lasted two hours and 40 minutes, 12 minutes shy of the running time of “The Odyssey.”

The arguments over the admissions policies of Harvard and the University of North Carolina, argued one after the other on a single Monday in 2022, stretched to almost five hours.

Asked about her strategy for covering that pair of arguments, Amy Howe, a reporter for Scotusblog, responded: “No liquids after 6 a.m.”

At a judicial conference in May, Chief Justice Roberts said he believed arguments have gotten “too long.” Addressing the problem, he said, was on the justices’ to-do list.

“I think we’ll have to look at it over the summer,” he said. The court, which will return to the bench in October, so far has not announced any changes.

Early in the court’s history, there were no time limits. The 1819 argument in McCulloch v. Maryland, which upheld the creation of a national bank, lasted nine days.

Since then the trend had been toward shorter arguments.

In 1849, the court capped arguments at two hours per side, for a total of four hours. Then, in 1925, the court cut that in half; in 1970, it again cut argument time in half.

That 30-minute time limit for each side was taken seriously, particularly by Chief Justice William H. Rehnquist, who led the court from 1986 to 2005. He would cut lawyers off in the middle of a sentence when they had used up their allotted time.

When Chief Justice Roberts took over, he was slightly more forgiving. But the basic format was unchanged until the pandemic. The typical argument was an unruly but productive commotion, with justices peppering the lawyers with questionsand often interrupting their answers and one another.

That changed in the spring of 2020. Unable to meet in person, the court cooked up a 20th- century solution to the 21st-century problem: they would hear arguments by telephone.

That medium, in which the justices and lawyers could hear but not see each other, did not allow for the dynamic free-for-all that had characterized arguments since at least the arrival of Justice Antonin Scalia in 1986. Instead, justices asked questions one at a time, in order of seniority. It was both civilized and inert.
